sec.t:
Korea was a single kingdom for centuries. Japan ruled it from 1910 to 1945. After the Second World War, the [[peninsula|peninsula]] was split between areas occupied by the Soviet Union in the north and the USA in the south. In 1950 the North invaded the South, and the Korean War drew in armies from many countries, part of the [[@cold-war|Cold War]].

The fighting stopped in 1953 with an armistice, an agreement to stop fighting, but no peace [[treaty|treaty]] was ever signed. A strip of land about 4 kilometres wide, the Demilitarised Zone or DMZ, still divides the two Koreas. With few people inside it for 70 years, it has become a refuge for cranes and other wildlife. Seoul is only about 50 kilometres from that border.

sec.h: An alphabet made by a king

sec.t:
Kimchi, spicy fermented cabbage with radish, garlic and chilli, appears at almost every meal. In late autumn, families and neighbours gather to make huge batches together, a tradition called kimjang that UNESCO lists as part of humanity's cultural heritage. The vegetables slowly [[@fermentation|ferment]] through the winter, turning sour and tangy, a little like an Indian [[@pickles-achar|achar]].

Korean homes have long been heated from below. In the old ondol system, smoke from a kitchen fire ran through channels under a stone floor. Modern homes use hot water pipes instead, which is why many Koreans sit, eat and even sleep on the warm floor.

In the middle of Seoul there was once a stream called Cheonggyecheon. As the city grew, it was covered with concrete and an elevated motorway was built on top. In 2003 the city tore down the motorway and dug the stream back out. It reopened in 2005 as a green walkway about 11 kilometres long, cooler than the streets around it. [[@urban-planning|City planners]] from many countries have visited to see how a road could be swapped for a river.

text: The Bible is the holy book of Christianity, the world's largest religion. Its first and longer part, often called the Old Testament, is also sacred to Jews, who call it the Tanakh or Hebrew Bible. The second part, the New Testament, is about the life and teachings of Jesus and his early followers.

It isn't one book written in one go. It is a library of dozens of books: laws, histories, poems, songs, wise sayings, prophecies and letters. Most were written in Hebrew or Greek, with some passages in Aramaic. Christians around the world read it in prayer and worship, and many believe it carries the word of God.

st.prompt: The word "Bible" comes from an ancient Greek word. What did that word mean?
st.reveal: Greek biblia means "books", or "little books". It came from Byblos, a port in today's Lebanon that traded papyrus, the paper of the ancient world. The name fits, since the Bible is a collection of many books.

src: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Bible.

Library of Congress, the Gutenberg Bible.
n.certNote: Christians and Jews hold the Bible to be sacred, and many believe it is inspired by God. Historians and religious scholars hold a range of views on who wrote each book and when, and these questions are still debated.

It is a collection of many writings, including history, laws, poems, songs, stories and letters. Many different writers produced them over a long period, and they were gathered together much later.

sec.t:
The Old Testament tells of the creation of the world, of Noah and the flood, and of Abraham, whom Jews, Christians and Muslims all honour. It follows Moses leading the Israelites out of slavery in Egypt, and young David defeating the giant Goliath. It includes the Psalms, a book of 150 poems and songs, and the words of prophets such as Isaiah.

The New Testament begins with four Gospels, each telling the story of Jesus in its own way. Then come the Acts of the Apostles and letters written to early Christian groups, many by a traveller and teacher named Paul. It ends with Revelation, a book of visions.

Different churches include slightly different books. Most Protestant Bibles have 66, Catholic Bibles have 73 and some Orthodox Bibles have a few more.

In 1947, Bedouin shepherds exploring caves at Qumran, near the [[@dead-sea|Dead Sea]], found clay jars holding ancient scrolls. Over the next years, searchers found fragments of hundreds of [[manuscript|manuscripts]]. Some had lain hidden for more than 2,000 years.

These Dead Sea Scrolls include the oldest known copies of books of the Hebrew Bible. A long scroll of Isaiah is almost complete. Scholars were struck by how closely it matches copies made about a thousand years later, showing how carefully scribes worked. Many fragments are now kept in [[@jerusalem|Jerusalem]], in a museum building whose white roof is shaped like the lid of one of the jars. Thousands of pieces have been photographed in high detail and can be viewed online by anyone.

Christians in Kerala have a tradition that Thomas, one of Jesus's twelve apostles, arrived there in 52 CE. Historians can't confirm this, but Christianity has certainly been in India for well over 1,500 years.

In 1714, a German missionary, Bartholomäus Ziegenbalg, printed the New Testament in Tamil at Tranquebar, one of the earliest Bible translations printed in an Indian language. Later, William Carey and his team at Serampore near Kolkata worked on translations into Bengali and many other languages.

The Bible has been [[@translation|translated]] more than almost any other book. By 2024, the full Bible existed in more than 700 languages, and parts of it in thousands more. In India, there are complete Bibles in Hindi, Tamil, Malayalam, Mizo, Khasi and dozens of other languages.

text: The Norse myths are the stories of the gods worshipped by the peoples of Scandinavia, the lands now called [[@norway-fjords|Norway]], Sweden and Denmark, and later Iceland. These were the people we often call [[@vikings|Vikings]]. Their gods included Odin the wise, Thor the thunderer, and Loki the shape-changing [[trickster|trickster]].

The myths tell how the world was made from [[@myths-giants|the body of a giant]], and how the gods fought giants and monsters. They also tell how it would all end, in a great battle called Ragnarok. Most of the stories survive because a few Icelandic writers recorded them about 800 years ago.

st.prompt: Which day of the week is named after Thor?
st.reveal: Thursday is "Thor's day". Wednesday comes from Woden, the English name for Odin, and Tuesday from Tyr, a god of war. Saturday is the odd one out, named after the Roman god Saturn.

src: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Germanic religion and mythology.
Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda (about 1220).

No Viking-age helmet with horns has ever been found. The horned look became popular in the 1800s, partly through costumes for Richard Wagner's operas based on Germanic myths.

sec.t:
Odin was the chief god, a wanderer who gave up one of his eyes to drink from a well of wisdom. Two ravens, Huginn and Muninn, whose names mean "thought" and "memory", flew round the world each day and told him what they saw.

Thor, Odin's son, was strong and short-tempered. With his hammer, Mjolnir, he protected gods and humans from giants. People wore small hammer-shaped charms, and [[archaeologist|archaeologists]] have found many of them. Freya was a goddess of love, gold and magic who rode in a chariot pulled by cats.

Loki is the hardest to pin down. Sometimes he helps the gods out of trouble with his cleverness. Sometimes he causes the trouble, and in the end he fights against them.

The Norse did write, using letters called runes, but runes were mostly carved as short messages on stone, wood or bone. The long stories were passed on by poets who learned them by heart.

After Scandinavia and [[@iceland|Iceland]] became Christian, around the year 1000, the old poems could easily have been forgotten. In about 1220, an Icelandic chieftain and scholar called Snorri Sturluson wrote the Prose Edda, partly as a guide for young poets who needed to understand the old stories. A collection of older poems, now called the Poetic Edda, survives in a [[manuscript|manuscript]] from the late 1200s. Most of what we know about Norse myths comes from these two works.

sec.h: Thor, Odin and the end of the world
sec.t:
The myths end with Ragnarok, the "fate of the gods". Winter lasts three years, monsters break free, and Thor and the great serpent of the sea kill each other. Then a new green world rises from the water, and a few gods and two humans survive to begin again.

The stories have travelled far. Just as the planets carry Roman names from the [[@greek-myths|Greek myths]], English weekdays carry Norse ones. Thor became a Marvel comic hero in 1962 and later a film star, part of the long story of [[@superheroes-history|superheroes]]. The comic Thor has blond hair, but the Thor of the old poems was usually described with a red beard.
